title: Maximize Total Cost of Alternating Subarrays
statement:
You get an integer array `nums`. Cut it into one or more non-empty contiguous pieces so that every element lands in exactly one piece; keeping the whole array as a single piece is allowed.

A piece `nums[l..r]` is worth its alternating sum that starts with a plus sign: `nums[l] - nums[l + 1] + nums[l + 2] - ...`, so the element at index `j` is multiplied by `(-1)^(j - l)`. Return the largest total worth of the pieces that any way of cutting can achieve.
notes:
## Intuition

Inside a piece, signs alternate starting with a plus. Cutting right before an element always gives it a plus, so the only real choice is which elements end up with a minus. An element can only be minus if the one before it is plus (it sits right after the start of a run of signs), and the very first element is always plus. So the task becomes: flip the signs of some elements, never two neighbours and never `nums[0]`, to make the sum as large as possible. Trying every cut is exponential; two running totals are enough.

## Approach

1. Keep `added`, the best total of the prefix when its last element is taken with a plus, and `subtracted`, the best when it is taken with a minus. At the start only `nums[0]` exists and it must be plus, so `added = nums[0]` and `subtracted = -Infinity`.
2. For each later `nums[i]`: a plus can follow either sign, so `nextAdded = max(added, subtracted) + nums[i]`.
3. A minus may only follow a plus, so `nextSubtracted = added - nums[i]`.
4. Move both new values into `added` and `subtracted`.
5. Return the larger of the two at the end.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, -2, 3, 4]`. Start with `added = 1`, `subtracted = -Infinity`.

- `i = 1` (`-2`): `added = 1 + (-2) = -1`, `subtracted = 1 - (-2) = 3`.
- `i = 2` (`3`): `added = max(-1, 3) + 3 = 6`, `subtracted = -1 - 3 = -4`.
- `i = 3` (`4`): `added = max(6, -4) + 4 = 10`, `subtracted = 6 - 4 = 2`.

The answer is `max(10, 2) = 10`, matching the pieces `[1, -2, 3]` and `[4]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass with constant work per element.
- Space: O(1): only two running totals.

## Pitfalls

- Update both states from the old values; overwriting `added` before computing `nextSubtracted` breaks the recurrence.
- The first element can never be subtracted, so `subtracted` must start as impossible, not `0` or `-nums[0]`.
- Totals reach about 10^14, beyond 32-bit integers; Java and C need `long`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `added` | best total so far with the current element taken as plus |
| `subtracted` | best total so far with the current element taken as minus |
| `i` | index of the element being added |
| `nextAdded`, `nextSubtracted` | the two states after including `nums[i]` |

narration.2: The first element always starts a piece, so it can only be added.
narration.3: No prefix can end with the first element subtracted, so this state starts as impossible.
narration.5: Extend the prefix one element at a time.
narration.6: Adding nums[i] is allowed after either sign, so take the better previous state.
narration.7: Subtracting nums[i] is only allowed right after an added element.
narration.8: Move the new states in, now that both were computed from the old ones.
narration.9: Store the subtracted state for the next step too.
narration.11: The last element may end with either sign; return the better total.
